Complementary information — The documents provide different facets: federal law entitlements, state variations, averages, and eligibility limitations, which together describe a complex landscape without contradiction.

The evidence clusters by scope and type: d2, d3, d5, d6, and d7 describe the federal FMLA entitlement of 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave [d3, d5, d6, d7], with d2 specifying 12 weeks of paid leave for federal employees. d1 and d6 mention state-level variations and additional provisions. d4 and d8 provide complementary context on averages and the lack of a federal paid mandate. These are non-contradictory pieces addressing different aspects of the query.

The supporting documents agree on a core federal entitlement of 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave under FMLA for eligible employees [d3, d5, d6, d7]. Document d2 adds that federal employees get 12 weeks of paid leave. Other documents complement this by noting state variations [d1, d6], average leave taken [d4], and the absence of a federal paid mandate [d8]. Together, they provide a multi-faceted answer.

In the United States, eligible mothers are entitled to up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) for the birth of a child [d3, d5, d6, d7]. However, this entitlement has significant limitations: many women do not qualify [d3], and the U.S. does not mandate paid maternity leave at the federal level [d8]. Some states have their own laws providing additional or paid leave [d1, d6], and federal employees are eligible for 12 weeks of paid parental leave [d2]. The average maternity leave taken is around 70 days [d4], which is less than international recommendations.
